title: Life on Earth depends on the networks of oceanic bacteria
text:
The original version of This story It appeared in Magazine how much .
Procllorococococcus Bacteria are so small that you would have to align around a thousand of them to coincide with the thickness of a human miniature. The ocean escapes with them: the microbes are likely to be The most abundant Photosynthetic organism on the planet, and create a significant portion, from 10 percent to 20 percent, of the oxygen of the atmosphere. That means that life on Earth depends on approximately 3 octillones (or 3 × 10 27 ) Small individual cells that work.
Biologists once thought of these organisms as isolated vagrants, drifting in unfathomable immensity. But the Procllorococococcus The population can be more connected than anyone could have imagined. They can be having conversations through wide distances, not only filling the ocean with information and nutrients, but also linking what we think were their private and internal spaces with the interiors of other cells.
At the University of Córdoba in Spain, not long ago, biologists who take images of cyanobacteria under a microscope saw a cell that had cultivated a long and thin tube and grabbed their neighbor. The image made them sit. He realized that this was not a coincidence.
“We realized that cyanobacteria were connected to each other,” he said María del Carmen Muñoz-Marín A microbiologist there. There were links between Procllorococococcus The cells, and also with another bacterium, called Synechococcus, that often lives nearby. In the images, the silver bridges linked three, four and more 10 or more cells.
Muñoz-Marín had a feeling on the identity of these mysterious structures. After a battery of tests, she and her colleagues Recently reported that these bridges are bacterial nanotubes. First observed in a common laboratory bacterium only 14 years ago, bacterial nanotubes are structures made of cell membrane that allow nutrients and resources to flow between two or more cells.
The structures have been A source of fascination and controversy During the last decade, as microbiologists have worked to understand what makes them form and what exactly travels between these network cells. The images of the Muñoz-Marín laboratory marked the first time that these structures have been seen in cyanobacteria responsible for much of the photosynthesis of the Earth.
They challenge the fundamental ideas about bacteria, asking questions such as: How much do you do? Procllorococococcus Do you share with the cells around you? And does it really make sense to think about it and other bacteria, such as a single cell?
Fully tubular Many bacteria have Active social lives . Some do PILI and sheet protein growths that link two cells to allow them to exchange DNA. Some form dense boards together, known as Biipels . And many emit small bubbles known as vesicles They contain DNA, RNA or other chemicals, such as messages in a bottle for any cell that interphens them.
There were vesicles that Muñoz-Marín and his colleagues, including José Manuel García-Fernández, a microbiologist at the University of Córdoba, and graduated student Elisa Angulo-Cánvas They were looking while they approached Procllorococococcus and Synechococcus In a plate. When they saw what they suspected they were Nanotubes, it was a surprise.
